description: We are the AstralMonkes, just a group of funny friends trying to last minute join the NASA Space apps and put our data analysis, UI/UX, and healthcare brains to good use. We bring the best of all worlds to the challenge, along with an ounce of imagination and a metric ton of delulu manifestation. (Please only join if I know you, don't join if I don't :) )
summary: HealthWings by AstralMonkes is a fun reimaging of how astronauts track and monitor their health. It divides their condition into sub systems across two branches, mental and physical, and provides, most significantly, the Health Wings panel at a glance, where the wings can tell them what they need to focus it. It has an AI chatbot, Dr. Pisces (he's not really a doctor), who astronauts can talk to in order to ask about symptoms and state of being. Based on the problem, it will decide the right test that they can do in zero gravity and gives them a pop-up card on how to perform it. Best of all, the keep astronauts motivated, the more they do tests and monitor their health, the more planets of the solar system they achieve. They could also lose planets if they grow neglectful.
details: The app uses fake placeholder data for the time being, all of which are user adjustable and initially local. They can use Google Sign-in to store their data on the cloud. It compares their diagnostic metrics to the standards shared by the NASA Lifetime Surveillance of Astronaut Health to calculate wellness. It also shows scatter plots of these metrics throughout history, with a shaded healthy region and an unshaded unhealthy region. It is written with React 19, Vite, Express, Tailwind CSS v4, and uses Lucide Icons & Google Fonts, along with Firebase support, browser-based Machine Learning and Gemini API access for the chatbot. The intended impact is to make health monitoring fun for astronauts and more like a game. We used the help of Gemini in Google AI Studio to bring our idea to life quickly. Our project considers the child in an astronaut and the number of things they're responsible for. We (and Dr. Pisces) want the experience to be fun, memorable, and engaging. We also considered different modes and color schemes, including a bioluminescent night version. The reason we went with a more ocean theme is to make the astronauts feel closer to home while still charting the unknown. We also wanted to make reminders pop up and made the tests as light based as possible, since those are barely different between Earth and Space. Overall, we made the app for our inner kid and imagined how lost we'd feel about our health out in the vast cosmos, when we're already lost enough here on Earth.
